title: Regularization & Optimization Basics
summary: The shared optimization and regularization toolkit that both classical ML and deep learning build on — why penalties fight overfitting, how gradient descent actually moves, and where it breaks.

slides.subTitle: Why penalize complexity
slides.markdown: Regularization fights **overfitting** by penalizing model complexity, not just training error. Give a model enough capacity and it memorizes noise in the training set instead of the underlying pattern, then fails on new data. The fix: add a penalty term to the loss so the optimizer is rewarded for staying simple — smaller weights, fewer active features — unless the data truly justifies more complexity. You trade a sliver of training accuracy for real gains on data the model has never seen.

slides.subTitle: L1 (Lasso) vs L2 (Ridge)
slides.markdown:
Both add a penalty on weight size to the loss, but the shape of that penalty changes the outcome.

| | L1 (Lasso) | L2 (Ridge) |
|---|---|---|
| Penalty | sum \|w\| | sum w² |
| Effect | zeroes out weights | shrinks weights smoothly |
| Result | sparse, built-in feature selection | keeps all features, none dominate |

L1's constraint region is a diamond with corners on the axes, so the optimum often lands on one, zeroing a weight. L2's region is a circle with no corners, so weights shrink but rarely hit zero. Pick L1 when many features are irrelevant; L2 when most carry signal.

slides.subTitle: The gradient descent update rule
slides.markdown: Gradient descent minimizes a loss function by repeatedly stepping opposite the gradient: **w := w - η·∇L(w)**, where η is the **learning rate**. The gradient points toward the steepest increase in loss, so subtracting it moves you downhill. η controls the step size: too large and updates overshoot the minimum, bouncing or diverging; too small and training converges correctly but crawls, wasting compute. There's no universal η — it's tuned per problem, and often decayed as training approaches the minimum.

slides.subTitle: Batch vs stochastic vs mini-batch
slides.markdown:
The three variants differ in how much data feeds each step. **Batch** uses the whole dataset — smooth descent, slow and memory-heavy. **SGD** uses one example per step — fast and noisy, sometimes escaping shallow dips. **Mini-batch**, the practical default, splits data into small batches, balancing accuracy against update speed.

slides.subTitle: Convex vs non-convex loss surfaces
slides.markdown: A **convex** loss surface is a single bowl — any local minimum is the global minimum, so gradient descent is guaranteed to reach it. Linear and logistic regression with standard losses are convex. Deep neural nets are **non-convex** — many local minima, saddle points, and plateaus. This matters less in practice than it sounds: in high-dimensional networks, most local minima found have loss close to the global optimum, and saddle points, not bad minima, are the more common obstacle — one that momentum-based optimizers navigate reasonably well.

slides.subTitle: Learning rate too high vs too low
slides.markdown: A learning rate set wrong quietly wrecks training either direction. **Too high**: updates overshoot the minimum and each correction overshoots further, so loss oscillates or explodes to NaN. **Too low**: training looks stable but crawls, needing far more epochs, and can stall on a plateau that's mistaken for convergence. The fix isn't guesswork — plot the loss curve, run a learning-rate range test, or apply a schedule (warmup then decay) so the rate matches the surface's sharpness at each stage.
